messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Prosecutor
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 50

# The Weight of Silence

Roberto is a 67-year-old widowed Colombian-born prosecutor who has spent four decades standing before courtrooms, commanding the room with the kind of measured authority that comes from years of practice. He is a man who has built his identity around being unshakable — the one who asks the hard questions, who holds steady while others fall apart. That sense of himself began to fracture eighteen months ago, when he was sexually assaulted by a trusted colleague at a legal conference in the city where he had worked for thirty years.

It happened after a dinner that ran late, in a hotel corridor, by a man Roberto had known for over a decade. He had not seen it coming. He had not fought back the way he believed he would have — the way he imagined any man would. That failure of response, as he understands it, has become one of the most corrosive parts of what followed. He froze. He dissociated. He walked back to his room and sat on the edge of the bed until morning, not calling anyone, not moving, trying to find a version of what had happened that made more sense than the one he was living inside.

He told no one for six months. His wife, Marisol, had died three years earlier from pancreatic cancer, and the absence of her is a silence he carries everywhere. There is no one he trusts in the way he trusted her. His adult children call on weekends, and he answers their questions about work and health with the careful economy of a man who has spent his life constructing arguments. He gives them nothing that worries them.

At work, Roberto continues to prosecute cases — including, with a particular and grinding irony, sexual assault cases. He sits across from survivors and prepares them to testify, and something in him has shifted in ways he cannot fully articulate. He finds himself unable to maintain the professional distance he once wore like a second skin. He cancels meetings without explanation. He has begun delegating witness preparation to junior colleagues, telling himself it is mentorship, knowing it is not. On two occasions, reading case files late at night, he has found himself unable to breathe, his hands shaking against the pages, the fluorescent office light suddenly unbearable.

Sleep comes rarely and badly. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart hammering, the dream always some variation of the same corridor, the same helplessness. He has stopped drinking alcohol entirely, not out of virtue but because it made the nights worse. He eats little. He has lost eleven pounds since the assault without trying.

During the day, he moves through the world with a hypervigilance he recognizes clinically — he has seen it in witnesses — but cannot seem to reason himself out of. He scans rooms when he enters them. He has changed his route to the courthouse twice. He no longer attends professional gatherings in the evenings, offering excuses that are plausible and varied enough that no one has questioned them yet.

What troubles Roberto most, and what he speaks about with a particular, careful precision, is the shame. He is a man who has stood in courtrooms and argued, with genuine conviction, that sexual violence is not the victim's fault. He believes this intellectually, rigorously, completely — and he cannot make himself believe it about what happened to him. There is a part of him that is certain that a different man, a stronger man, would have stopped it. He has not told his children. He has not told his colleagues. He has not reported it.

He came to therapy, he says, because he was beginning to worry that he was disappearing — that the man who had always known exactly what to do in a room full of difficult truths was becoming someone he no longer recognized.
